source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 16: India, Physical Features
fact_summary: India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern hemispheres. The mainland extends approximately from 8°4′N to 37°6′N latitude and 68°7′E to 97°25′E longitude. The Tropic of Cancer, 23°30′N, crosses the country roughly through its middle, while the standard meridian is 82°30′E. The north–south mainland extent is about 3,214 km and the east–west extent about 2,933 km. India covers about 3.28 million square kilometres. The southernmost point of the mainland is Kanyakumari; Indira Point in the Nicobar group is the southernmost point of Indian territory. Latitude controls north–south position, longitude east–west position, and one degree of longitude represents four minutes of local solar time.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS India physical-features lesson; stable coordinate and extent facts only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 16: India, Physical Features
fact_summary: India's land neighbours are Pakistan and Afghanistan to the north-west, China, Nepal and Bhutan to the north, and Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east. Sri Lanka and Maldives are maritime neighbours. Sri Lanka is separated from the Indian mainland by the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar. Bangladesh is bordered by the Indian states of West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Nepal adjoins Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim; Bhutan adjoins Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh. The Arabian Sea lies to the west, Bay of Bengal to the east and Indian Ocean to the south. A land boundary and a maritime boundary must not be treated as the same relationship.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS India geography lesson; stable neighbour and surrounding-water facts only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 16: India, Physical Features
fact_summary: India's major physiographic divisions are the Northern Mountains, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the Coastal Plains and the Islands. The Himalayas are young fold mountains and include parallel ranges; the Northern Plains were built largely by alluvium deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems. The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient stable block and includes the Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau. The Western Ghats form a more continuous, generally higher escarpment than the discontinuous Eastern Ghats. The Thar Desert lies mainly west of the Aravalli range. The western coastal plain is generally narrower than the eastern coastal plain, where large river deltas are common.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Chapter 16 description of India's physiographic divisions.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 16: India, Physical Features
fact_summary: The western coast faces the Arabian Sea and includes the Konkan, Kannad or Karnataka, and Malabar sections; the eastern coast faces the Bay of Bengal and includes the Northern Circars and Coromandel Coast. Lakshadweep is a coral-island group in the Arabian Sea, while the Andaman and Nicobar groups lie in the Bay of Bengal. The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman group from the Nicobar group. Indian Standard Time is based on 82°30′E longitude, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC. The meridian passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Because India spans almost 29 degrees of longitude, local solar time differs by nearly two hours between the eastern and western extremes, but one standard time is used nationally.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS India geography lesson; stable coast, island, and standard-time facts only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 21: Our Water Resources
fact_summary: The three major Himalayan river systems are the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra. They receive water from rain and snow or glacier melt and are generally perennial. The Indus rises near the Tibetan plateau and its important Himalayan tributaries include Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. The Ganga begins as the Bhagirathi from the Gangotri glacier and takes the name Ganga after meeting the Alaknanda at Devprayag; Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and Son are major tributaries. The Brahmaputra is known as the Tsangpo in Tibet, enters India through Arunachal Pradesh and flows through Assam before reaching Bangladesh. Himalayan rivers form meanders, floodplains and extensive alluvial deposits in the plains.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS water-resources lesson; stable Himalayan drainage facts only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 21: Our Water Resources
fact_summary: Most Peninsular rivers are rain-fed, follow older fixed valleys and show greater seasonal variation than Himalayan rivers. The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow generally eastward into the Bay of Bengal and form deltas. The Godavari has the largest basin among Peninsular rivers and is often called the Dakshin Ganga. Narmada and Tapi flow westward through rift valleys and form estuaries rather than large deltas. The Western Ghats are a major water divide: many short swift streams descend to the Arabian Sea, while longer east-flowing systems cross the plateau. Chambal, Betwa and Ken are important tributaries of the Yamuna but originate in the Peninsular uplands.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS water-resources lesson; stable Peninsular drainage facts only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 21: Our Water Resources
fact_summary: A drainage basin or catchment is the land area from which a river and its tributaries collect runoff. A watershed or water divide is the elevated boundary separating neighbouring drainage basins. Tributaries join a main river, while distributaries branch away from it, commonly in a delta. Drainage patterns reflect slope and rock structure: dendritic resembles tree branches on broadly uniform rock, trellis develops where hard and soft strata guide tributaries, radial flows outward from a central highland, and centripetal converges into an inland basin. Basin management must consider upstream and downstream links because land use, erosion, storage and pollution in one part can affect water quantity and quality elsewhere.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS water-resources lesson; basin, divide, and drainage-pattern definitions only.

source_title: NIOS Geography — Chapter 21: Our Water Resources
fact_summary: Multipurpose river projects can support irrigation, hydroelectricity, flood moderation, municipal or industrial water supply, navigation and fisheries, but can also displace communities, trap sediment and alter ecosystems. Bhakra-Nangal is on the Sutlej, Hirakud on the Mahanadi, Tehri on the Bhagirathi, Sardar Sarovar on the Narmada and Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna. Canal irrigation is important in level alluvial plains; wells and tube wells use groundwater; tanks are common where undulating hard-rock terrain favours local storage. Watershed development, rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation, aquifer recharge, pollution control and demand management complement large storage. Water conservation must match local rainfall, geology and use.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS water-resources lesson; stable project-location and management concepts only.

source_title: Reserve Bank of India Annual Report — The Reserve Bank's Accounts
fact_summary: The Reserve Bank of India was established under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, began operations on 1 April 1935 and was nationalised in 1949. It is India's central bank and monetary authority. Core functions include issuing most currency notes, formulating and implementing monetary policy, regulating and supervising banks and parts of the financial system, managing foreign-exchange reserves, overseeing payment and settlement systems, acting as banker to banks and to government, managing public debt and supporting financial stability and development. The one-rupee note and coins are issued by the Government of India, although coins are put into circulation through the Reserve Bank. RBI's Central Office was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937.
verification_notes: Reviewed against RBI's official institutional and annual-report material; stable statutory and functional facts only.

source_title: NIOS Economics — Chapter 28: Money and Banking
fact_summary: Commercial banks accept deposits, provide loans and advances, create deposit money through lending, and facilitate payments and remittances. Primary deposit types include demand deposits, withdrawable on demand, and time or term deposits, held for an agreed period. Savings and current accounts are demand-deposit forms; fixed and recurring deposits are term-deposit forms. Banks provide cash credit, overdraft, term loans, bill discounting and other credit according to purpose and risk. They also offer agency services such as collecting instruments or paying standing instructions, and utility services such as cards, electronic transfers and lockers. Credit creation is constrained by reserve requirements, liquidity, capital, borrower demand, repayment risk and central-bank policy.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Money and Banking chapter; stable commercial-bank functions only.

micro_topic_name: Repo, Reverse Repo, CRR ও SLR
source_title: Reserve Bank of India — Liquidity Adjustment Facility and Current Rates
fact_summary: The policy repo rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank supplies overnight liquidity to eligible entities against government and other approved securities under the liquidity framework. A reverse-repo transaction absorbs liquidity when the Reserve Bank receives funds and provides securities; the fixed reverse-repo rate is distinct from the Standing Deposit Facility, which absorbs liquidity without collateral. Cash Reserve Ratio is the prescribed share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities maintained as cash balance with RBI. Statutory Liquidity Ratio is the prescribed share maintained by banks in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved securities. Raising liquidity-absorption requirements generally reduces lendable resources; current numeric rates are deliberately excluded because they change by policy decision.
verification_notes: Reviewed against RBI's official liquidity-facility and reserve-ratio material; definitions only, with no mutable rate values.

source_title: Reserve Bank of India — Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Norms
fact_summary: A savings account is a demand deposit intended for saving with applicable transaction conditions; a current account is a demand deposit allowing frequent business transactions; a fixed deposit is kept for an agreed term; and a recurring deposit builds a term deposit through periodic instalments. A loan creates an obligation to repay principal with agreed interest, whereas an overdraft permits withdrawal up to a sanctioned limit. Under RBI asset-classification norms, a term loan generally becomes a non-performing asset when interest or principal remains overdue for more than 90 days; overdraft or cash-credit accounts use the prescribed 'out of order' test. NPAs are classified into substandard, doubtful and loss categories under applicable norms, and banks make provisions against expected loss.
verification_notes: Reviewed against RBI's official deposit definitions and IRAC norms; stable account and NPA concepts only.

source_title: MoSPI FAQs — Consumer Price Indices and Inflation
fact_summary: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, commonly measured as the percentage change in a representative price index over time; a one-time increase in one item's price is not by itself economy-wide inflation. Demand-pull inflation can arise when aggregate demand grows faster than available output. Cost-push inflation can arise from higher wages, energy, raw-material, tax or transport costs that firms pass through to prices. Supply shocks such as crop failure or disrupted imports can raise selected prices and spread more widely. Expansion of money and credit beyond real output can support persistent demand pressure. Headline inflation uses the broad basket, while core measures exclude selected volatile components for analytical purposes; classifications describe mechanisms, not mutually exclusive events.
verification_notes: Reviewed against MoSPI's official inflation FAQ and Government of India inflation analysis; stable definitions and mechanisms only.

source_title: MoSPI — Consumer Price Index
fact_summary: Consumer Price Index measures change over time in prices of a selected basket of goods and services acquired by households for consumption. India's NSO releases CPI for Rural, Urban and Combined sectors; the current established series uses 2012=100 and the all-India basket contains 299 weighted items. CPI inflation is usually calculated from the year-on-year percentage change in the index. Wholesale Price Index tracks prices at the wholesale or producer-facing stage and differs from CPI in coverage and weights; it is not a household cost-of-living index. A price index compares a weighted basket with a base period: an index of 120 means the weighted price level is 20 percent above the base, not that inflation in the latest year is automatically 20 percent.
verification_notes: Reviewed against MoSPI's official CPI portal and FAQ; methodology facts only, no current index readings.

source_title: Reserve Bank of India Annual Report — Economic Review: Prices
fact_summary: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money: if nominal income does not keep pace, a household can buy fewer goods and services. Unexpected inflation tends to hurt fixed-income receivers and lenders while reducing the real burden of fixed nominal debt for borrowers. It can distort saving, investment, contracts and price signals, and volatile food or fuel inflation can affect groups differently because expenditure baskets differ. Moderate predictable inflation and high or accelerating inflation do not have identical effects; uncertainty itself raises planning costs. Nominal interest is stated in money terms, while a simplified real-interest approximation subtracts expected inflation. Indexation can partly protect wages, pensions or contracts, but it may also transmit price changes. Policy responses involve demand, liquidity, supply and fiscal trade-offs.
verification_notes: Reviewed against RBI's official prices and inflation analysis; general distributional and real-value effects only.

source_title: Reserve Bank of India Annual Report — Economic Review: Prices
fact_summary: Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level, represented by a negative inflation rate. Disinflation is a reduction in a still-positive inflation rate: prices continue to rise, but more slowly. Reflation refers to policy or recovery that lifts demand and the price level from deflationary weakness toward a desired path. Stagflation combines high inflation with stagnant or weak output and high unemployment, making policy difficult because measures that restrain demand may weaken activity further. A fall in inflation from 8 percent to 5 percent is disinflation, not deflation; a price index falling year on year indicates deflation. A lower individual commodity price is neither condition unless it affects the general index. Base effects can change a measured rate without an equivalent current-period price movement.
verification_notes: Reviewed against RBI's official inflation analysis; stable distinctions among price-level concepts only.

source_title: NIOS Indian Culture and Heritage — Chapter 3: Ancient India
fact_summary: Prehistory is studied mainly through material remains because written records are absent. The Palaeolithic is associated with chipped stone tools and hunting-gathering; the Mesolithic with microliths and transitional subsistence; the Neolithic with polished tools, cultivation and settled village life. The Harappan or Indus civilisation was an urban Bronze Age culture with planned streets, drainage, standardised weights, craft production and long-distance trade. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are in present-day Pakistan; Dholavira is in Kutch, Lothal in Gujarat, Kalibangan in Rajasthan and Rakhigarhi in Haryana. Harappan writing remains undeciphered. The Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira is noted for reservoirs, and Lothal is associated with a dock-like basin.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ancient India lesson; stable archaeological-period and Harappan-site facts only.

source_title: NIOS Indian Culture and Heritage — Chapter 3: Ancient India
fact_summary: The Rigveda is the earliest of the four Vedas; the others are Sama, Yajur and Atharva. Early Vedic society was largely pastoral with cattle important to wealth, while later Vedic life saw wider agriculture, iron use and territorial kingdoms in the Ganga-Yamuna region. Sabha and Samiti appear as assemblies in Vedic literature. The basic social and political units are described through family, grama, vis and jana, though their roles changed over time. Early worship centred on deities connected with natural and social forces such as Indra, Agni and Varuna; later texts developed elaborate ritual and philosophical inquiry. Brahmanas explain ritual, Aranyakas are forest texts and Upanishads explore concepts including atman and brahman. Vedic periods must not be treated as socially static.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ancient India lesson; stable textual and broad social-change facts only.

source_title: NIOS Indian Culture and Heritage — Chapter 3: Ancient India
fact_summary: Sixteen Mahajanapadas are listed for roughly the sixth century BCE; Magadha rose through resources, strategic location and rulers of dynasties including Haryanka, Shishunaga and Nanda. Gautama Buddha was born at Lumbini, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave the first sermon at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar. Buddhist teaching centres on the Four Noble Truths and Noble Eightfold Path and rejects both extreme indulgence and extreme austerity. Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara of Jain tradition, taught right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Jainism gives central importance to ahimsa, aparigraha and anekantavada. Early Buddhist literature includes the Tripitaka; Jain traditions preserved teachings in Agamas. Both traditions used accessible languages and developed monastic communities.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ancient India lesson; stable Mahajanapada, Buddhist, and Jain fundamentals only.

micro_topic_name: মৌর্য, গুপ্ত ও দক্ষিণ ভারতের রাজবংশ
source_title: NIOS Indian Culture and Heritage — Chapter 3: Ancient India
fact_summary: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire with Chanakya or Kautilya associated with his rise; Megasthenes visited his court. Ashoka embraced and promoted dhamma after the Kalinga war, communicating through rock and pillar edicts in several scripts and languages. The Gupta period included rulers such as Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II; the Allahabad pillar inscription praises Samudragupta. Aryabhata contributed to mathematics and astronomy, Kalidasa to Sanskrit literature, and Gupta art is represented at sites including Sarnath and Ajanta's contemporary florescence. In the south, Sangam literature illuminates the Chera, Chola and Pandya polities; Pallavas centred on Kanchipuram and later Cholas developed a powerful state, temples and maritime connections.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ancient India lesson; stable ruler, inscription, culture, and southern-polity facts only.

source_title: NIOS Social Science — Chapter 8: Indian National Movement
fact_summary: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885; its first session met in Bombay under W. C. Bonnerjee, with A. O. Hume associated with its organisation. Early nationalists or Moderates included Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjea, Pherozeshah Mehta and Gopal Krishna Gokhale. They used petitions, resolutions, public meetings and constitutional argument to press for representative institutions, civil rights, Indianisation of services and economic reform. Naoroji's drain theory explained how colonial mechanisms transferred wealth from India. Economic criticism, newspapers, associations, modern education and political debate helped create an all-India public sphere. The early phase built organisation and national consciousness even though later leaders criticised its limited methods.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Indian National Movement lesson; stable foundation, leader, method, and economic-critique facts only.

source_title: NIOS Social Science — Chapter 8: Indian National Movement
fact_summary: The 1905 partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon triggered the Swadeshi and Boycott movements, encouraging indigenous goods, national education and mass protest. The partition was annulled in 1911. Assertive nationalist leaders are often associated with Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. The Congress split at Surat in 1907. Revolutionary organisations and individuals used clandestine methods in Bengal, Maharashtra, Punjab and abroad, while the Ghadar movement mobilised expatriate networks. During 1916, Tilak and Annie Besant led separate Home Rule Leagues demanding self-government, and the Lucknow Pact brought Congress and the Muslim League to an agreement. These strands differed in method and should not be conflated.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Indian National Movement lesson; stable Swadeshi, revolutionary, and Home Rule chronology only.

source_title: NIOS Social Science — Chapter 8: Indian National Movement
fact_summary: Gandhi's early Indian satyagrahas included Champaran in 1917 concerning indigo cultivators, Ahmedabad mill workers in 1918 and Kheda peasants in 1918. The Rowlatt Act agitation and Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred in 1919. The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920 alongside the Khilafat issue and was withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura violence in 1922. Civil Disobedience began with the 1930 Dandi March against the salt law; the Gandhi-Irwin Pact preceded Gandhi's participation in the Second Round Table Conference. The movement resumed and later waned. Satyagraha emphasised truth and non-violent resistance, while programmes included boycott, constructive work and wider participation by peasants, workers, students and women.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Indian National Movement lesson; stable Gandhian chronology and method facts only.

micro_topic_name: আজাদ হিন্দ, ভারত ছাড়ো ও স্বাধীনতা
source_title: NIOS Social Science — Chapter 8: Indian National Movement
fact_summary: The Congress launched the Quit India Movement in Bombay in August 1942 after the failure of the Cripps Mission; Gandhi gave the 'Do or Die' call and the leadership was quickly arrested, but protests continued in decentralised forms. Subhas Chandra Bose assumed leadership of the Indian National Army in Southeast Asia and proclaimed the Provisional Government of Azad Hind in 1943; the INA campaigns and later Red Fort trials had major political impact. The Cabinet Mission came in 1946, followed by negotiations amid communal conflict. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 created the independent dominions of India and Pakistan; British rule ended on 15 August 1947. Partition caused mass displacement and violence, so independence and partition are linked but distinct historical processes.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Indian National Movement lesson; stable Quit India, INA, and transfer-of-power facts only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 5: Ecosystem
fact_summary: An ecosystem is a functional unit in which a community of organisms interacts with the physical environment through energy flow and nutrient cycling. Abiotic components include light, temperature, water, air, soil and mineral nutrients. Biotic components include producers, consumers and decomposers. Producers convert solar or chemical energy into organic matter; consumers obtain energy by feeding; decomposers and detritivores break down dead material and return nutrients. Habitat is the place an organism lives, while ecological niche describes its role and resource use. Ecosystems may be natural or human-modified and terrestrial or aquatic. Productivity is the rate of biomass or energy production; gross primary productivity includes all fixation and net primary productivity remains after producers' respiration.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ecosystem lesson; stable structure, role, and productivity definitions only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 5: Ecosystem
fact_summary: A food chain is a linear feeding pathway, and each step is a trophic level. A grazing chain begins with living green plants, passes to herbivores and then carnivores; a detritus chain begins with dead organic matter and proceeds through decomposers or detritivores. A food web interconnects multiple food chains and better represents real ecosystems because organisms may use several foods or occupy different levels. Arrows in a food-chain diagram conventionally point in the direction of energy transfer, from the resource or prey toward the consumer. Producers form the first trophic level in a grazing chain, primary consumers the second and secondary consumers the next. Omnivores can connect levels, while removal of a strongly connected species can produce indirect effects across the web.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ecosystem lesson; food-chain, food-web, and trophic-level facts only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 5: Ecosystem
fact_summary: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, is fixed by producers and moves through consumers and decomposers. At every transfer, much energy is used in metabolism and lost as heat, so energy flow is unidirectional and available energy declines at higher trophic levels. The ecological 'ten percent law' is a useful approximate teaching rule, not an exact value for every ecosystem. A pyramid of energy shows energy flow per area per time and is always upright. A pyramid of biomass may be upright on land but inverted in some aquatic systems where rapidly renewing phytoplankton support greater standing consumer biomass. A pyramid of numbers may be upright or inverted depending on organism size and life history. Nutrients cycle, but energy does not recycle.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ecosystem lesson; energy-flow and ecological-pyramid principles only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 5: Ecosystem
fact_summary: Biogeochemical cycles move matter between organisms and air, water, soil or rock. In the water cycle, evaporation and transpiration add vapour, condensation forms clouds, precipitation returns water, and infiltration, groundwater flow and runoff redistribute it. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide and stores carbon in organic matter; respiration, decomposition and combustion release carbon dioxide. Most organisms cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly: fixation converts it to usable compounds, nitrification changes ammonium to nitrites and nitrates, assimilation builds organic nitrogen, ammonification returns ammonium and denitrification returns nitrogen gas. The phosphorus cycle is mainly sedimentary and lacks a major gaseous phase. Human combustion, fertiliser use and land change can alter cycle rates.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Ecosystem lesson; major water, carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus-cycle steps only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 15: Biodiversity Conservation
fact_summary: Biodiversity includes variation at genetic, species and ecosystem levels. Genetic diversity is variation within a species or population and supports adaptation, breeding and resilience. Species diversity includes both richness, the number of species, and evenness, how individuals are distributed among species. Ecosystem diversity is the variety of habitats, ecological communities and processes across a landscape. Alpha diversity describes diversity within a site, beta diversity change between sites, and gamma diversity the broader regional total. Biodiversity supplies food, fibre, medicines, pollination, soil formation, water regulation and cultural values. Loss at one level can affect the others, and a large number of organisms alone does not necessarily mean high species diversity if nearly all belong to one species.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Biodiversity Conservation lesson; diversity-level and value definitions only.

source_title: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change — Biodiversity
fact_summary: A biodiversity hotspot is a global conservation-priority region with exceptional endemic plant richness and severe habitat loss; it is not simply any place with many species. Parts of India fall within four globally recognised hotspots: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Sundaland, represented in India by the Nicobar Islands. A hotspot's boundary can cross national borders. The Eastern Himalaya is part of the Himalaya hotspot, north-eastern India largely overlaps Indo-Burma, and the Western Ghats form India's portion of the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka hotspot. Endemism means a taxon is naturally restricted to a defined area. Hotspot status prioritises threatened concentrations of unique biodiversity but does not replace protection of other ecosystems.
verification_notes: Reviewed against MoEFCC biodiversity material; stable hotspot definition and India-region mappings only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 15: Biodiversity Conservation
fact_summary: An endemic species is native to and naturally restricted to a particular geographic area; it is not automatically endangered. A threatened species faces elevated extinction risk, with formal categories assessed under stated criteria; endangered indicates a higher risk than vulnerable, while critically endangered is higher still. Extinction means no surviving individual remains, whereas local extinction or extirpation is loss from only part of the range. An alien species occurs outside its natural range through human action; it becomes invasive when it establishes, spreads and causes ecological, economic or health harm. Major pressures include habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, climate change and disease. Small range, low population and specialised habitat can increase vulnerability.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Biodiversity Conservation lesson; status and invasion definitions only.

source_title: NIOS Environmental Science — Chapter 15: Biodiversity Conservation
fact_summary: In-situ conservation protects species in their natural ecosystems and maintains ecological interactions and evolution; national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, community reserves and gene sanctuaries are examples. Ex-situ conservation maintains components outside their natural habitat through zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks, tissue culture, cryopreservation or captive breeding. In-situ is generally preferred for whole ecosystems and many interacting species, while ex-situ can support species with extremely small populations, provide genetic backup and enable planned reintroduction. A biosphere reserve combines conservation with research and sustainable-use zones; a seed bank is ex-situ even though seeds originated in the wild. Neither approach alone removes the need to control habitat loss, illegal use, disease and genetic erosion.
verification_notes: Reviewed against the official NIOS Biodiversity Conservation lesson; in-situ and ex-situ distinctions only.
